profile.bio: Ashutosh Pal Singh. Cyber security analyst across security monitoring, vulnerability management, application security testing and incident investigation; MSc Cyber Security Engineering (University of Warwick, NCSC certified), Microsoft SC-200. These projects measure the error rates behind detection rules, vulnerability scanners, blockchain investigations and forensic timelines. Based in the UK, open to roles in blockchain analytics and crypto investigations, DFIR, fraud and financial crime, SOC, vulnerability management and security research.

projects.title: evm-cluster-check
projects.oneLine: How often published Ethereum clustering and taint rules link addresses that belong to two different exchanges, and what causes it.
projects.headline: On 3 days of Ethereum (5.44M transactions), naive deposit-address reuse merged 198 pairs of addresses from two different exchanges, none caused by poisoning, sweepers or fee services; the same-sender rule merged 359, and 60% of those came only through poisoning transfers.

metrics.label: Cross-exchange false merges, deposit-address reuse
Share of deposit-reuse false merges caused by infrastructure
Cross-exchange false merges, same sender in one tx
Share of same-sender false merges caused by poisoning

proof.label: Cross-exchange false merges by deposit-address reuse

charts.label: False merges by rule
charts.alt: Bar chart of cross-exchange false merges per clustering rule, with hubs included and excluded

charts.label: Causes
charts.alt: Share of false merges that disappear when poisoning, sweeper and paymaster transfers are removed

charts.label: Taint
charts.alt: Addresses tainted at 1 to 3 hops, with and without zero-value transfers

charts.label: Injected tests
charts.alt: False links made by each rule on wallets I control on a local fork

misses: Binance and Bitstamp publish their reserve lists only on their own sites, which I could not reach, so every false merge count is a lower bound.
Only one free provider served Ethereum logs, so the token transfer data has no second source. chain-evidence checked 40 blocks of it instead.
The taint stage ran the machine out of memory and lost a run. It now keeps one slim table and resumes from saved stages.
The 20 sampled false merges were classified by script, not opened one by one on a block explorer.

viz.title: Naive deposit reuse and the same-sender rule wrongly merge addresses of two different exchanges
Poisoning and other infrastructure cause most same-sender false merges and none from deposit reuse
Zero-value transfers inflate the addresses a one-hop taint rule flags

projects.title: timetruth
projects.oneLine: Scripted actions at known times, then a check of whether mainstream forensic tools report those times correctly.
projects.headline: 1828 tool-reported times checked (16 runs: 4 file systems x 4 time-zone scenarios x 30 actions, 6 tool configurations). 502 (27%) were not the true instant: 264 wrong value, 146 right clock reading in the wrong zone, 76 ambiguous, 16 missing.

metrics.label: Tool-reported times checked
Times not the true instant
Times correct on FAT32
Times correct on NTFS

proof.label: Forensic tool times that were not the true instant

charts.label: Outcome by tool
charts.alt: Stacked bars of each tool’s reported times by outcome: correct, wrong zone, ambiguous, wrong value or missing

charts.label: Correct by file system
charts.alt: Heat map of the percentage of reported times that are the true instant, per tool, file system and time zone scenario

charts.label: Clock changes
charts.alt: TSK fls reported minus true time around the London and New York clock changes, and Plaso’s offset of about 30 days on FAT32 and exFAT

charts.label: Pipeline
charts.alt: Flow from scripted actions through a fake clock, disk image, the tools under test and a common schema to the classifier

misses: libfaketime also shifted stat() results, so my first NTFS run applied the offset twice. Fixed with NO_FAKE_STAT=1.
MFTECmd would not run under Mono, so analyzeMFT stands in on Linux and is labelled that way everywhere.
Every image was written by a Linux driver. The Windows kit that would test real Windows writes has not been run yet.
ext4 ignores libfaketime, so the ext4 “DST” runs did not actually cross a clock change.

viz.title: Only ext4 and NTFS times are reported correctly almost every time
Of 1,828 reported times, about a quarter were not the true instant
Only analyzeMFT reports every time correctly; Plaso reports the fewest

projects.title: chain-evidence
projects.oneLine: Ask several independent providers for the same on chain data, flag any disagreement, and prove completeness against the block header.
projects.headline: Across 524 finalised Ethereum block ranges asked of three free RPC providers, every recent range agreed (383/383), but on older blocks a provider silently returned nothing where receipt proofs show 286 logs (2/20 comparable ranges), and publicnode returned `null` receipts for 7/7 sampled transactions older than ~6 days.

metrics.label: Ethereum finalised ranges compared
Ethereum disagreement rate
Ethereum empty successes (0 logs where logs exist)
Ethereum blocks from drpc whose receipts reproduce receiptsRoot

proof.label: Silent empty answers where receipt proofs show logs

charts.label: Provider outcomes
charts.alt: Stacked bars of what each provider returned on Ethereum and Base: matching, differing or uncompared answers, refusals and failures

charts.label: Disagreement rate
charts.alt: Share of finalised Ethereum ranges that disagreed in each of three runs, with 95% Wilson intervals; the worst run was 2 of 161

charts.label: Finalized tag lag
charts.alt: Most blocks each provider’s finalized head fell behind the most advanced provider, up to 17,376 for 1rpc on Base

charts.label: Receipts root proofs
charts.alt: Blocks per provider whose header hash, transactionsRoot and receiptsRoot reproduce; none mismatched, publicnode returned null receipts for 5 blocks

charts.label: Receipt depth
charts.alt: publicnode receipts by block age: 63 returned up to about 6 days behind the finalised head, 7 null beyond that

misses: I deleted the bundle of the first silent empty answer while resetting results. It is recorded in my notes and not counted.
1rpc ran out of free quota and relays publicnode, so most Ethereum comparisons are only two way.
My first probe said publicnode serves deep receipts. It counted a null answer as success.
mainnet.base.org refuses eth_getLogs, so Base has receipt proofs but no log comparison.

viz.title: Recent blocks always agreed; older blocks did not
Most answers from three Ethereum providers matched; refusals were the main failure
Only older ranges silently missed logs that receipt proofs show exist

projects.title: rulefire
projects.oneLine: Do Sigma rules fire on the attack they were written for? Every rule run against public attack recordings and benign Windows logs.
projects.headline: 2 small open models running on CPU wrote 252 Sigma rules for 63 ATT&CK techniques: 53.2% parsed as YAML, 0 loaded as valid Sigma and 0 fired on public attack captures of their technique; one SigmaHQ rule per technique fires on 23.1%.

charts.label: Executor check
charts.alt: SigmaHQ regression tests passed by the rulefire executor

charts.label: Pipeline
charts.alt: Diagram of the rulefire pipeline from task list and rules to execution and scoring

misses: Only two small open models ran (qwen2.5-coder 3B and llama3.2 3B), one sample per technique, on a CPU. Larger models, five samples per technique, the repair loop and any hosted model were not run.
The benign logs are the set SigmaHQ already tests against, so its near zero false alarm rate is not a fair comparison for untuned rules.
196 technique and capture pairs from EVTX-ATTACK-SAMPLES are my own mapping, because that collection has no technique IDs.
My first Security 4688 pipeline never matched anything. It was fixed before the published run, with six other harness bugs listed.

viz.title: Where all model rules fail: before they ever run
The coder model writes YAML far more often, and the log-source list helps both
Rules that fire on their technique: one SigmaHQ rule 23.1%, models none

projects.title: fixproof
projects.oneLine: Do vulnerability scanners say fixed while the old vulnerable code is still running? 22 public CVEs on 8 Linux images, each host state built 3 times.
projects.headline: On hosts updated but not restarted, 138 of 138 scanner verdicts (100.0%) said fixed while the old vulnerable code was still running; 2 of 2 scanners did so every time.

charts.alt: Truth against verdict counts for each scanner

charts.label: Restart detectors
charts.alt: Share of processes running stale vulnerable code that needrestart and Vuls flagged

misses: Only Trivy and OSV-Scanner were scored. OpenVAS, Wazuh, Grype and OpenSCAP could not run in the lab.
The hosts are containers, so the new kernel installed but old kernel running state could not be built.
Only the Ubuntu hosts were upgraded with apt. Debian, Alpine, Rocky and Alma used an image overlay.
The Vuls restart check needs sudo and could not run on 21 of 38 host states.

viz.title: Updated but not restarted: share of verdicts that said fixed while old code ran
Restart detectors: share of stale vulnerable programs they flagged
Backported fixes: version-string checks cry wolf

projects.title: logcanary
projects.oneLine: Numbered canary events written through rsyslog and journald, then counted again in Elasticsearch, to measure how many logs Filebeat, Fluent Bit and Vector lose under faults, and whether anything says so.
projects.headline: 1,561,800 numbered canaries written through rsyslog and journald on an Ubuntu 24.04 host and counted again in Elasticsearch across 25 conditions: default pipelines lost up to 84.8% (Fluent Bit, Elasticsearch stopped for 10 min), and 82 of 124 lossy streams left no log line anywhere saying events were lost.

misses: Elasticsearch throttled indexing in 56 of the 88 runs because the build disk was nearly full. Those runs are flagged in every table and the lab now sets the disk watermark; I did not rerun them.
The Ubuntu 22.04 host is defined in code but was not run, and neither were auditd, Windows or Splunk.
The raw ledgers and arrival files (76 MB) are kept out of git. Their hashes are published, but without them the latency, timeline and clock charts cannot be redrawn from the repository alone.
In the +2 h clock runs journald restarted about once a second, which may be caused by the fake-clock tool rather than by journald.

out: On 3 days of Ethereum (5.44M transactions), naive deposit-address reuse merged 198 pairs of addresses from two different exchanges, none caused by poisoning, sweepers or fee services; the same-sender rule merged 359, and 60% of those came only through poisoning transfers.

1828 tool-reported times checked (16 runs: 4 file systems x 4 time-zone scenarios x 30 actions, 6 tool configurations). 502 (27%) were not the true instant: 264 wrong value, 146 right clock reading in the wrong zone, 76 ambiguous, 16 missing.

Across 524 finalised Ethereum block ranges asked of three free RPC providers, every recent range agreed (383/383), but on older blocks a provider silently returned nothing where receipt proofs show 286 logs (2/20 comparable ranges), and publicnode returned `null` receipts for 7/7 sampled transactions older than ~6 days.

2 small open models running on CPU wrote 252 Sigma rules for 63 ATT&CK techniques: 53.2% parsed as YAML, 0 loaded as valid Sigma and 0 fired on public attack captures of their technique; one SigmaHQ rule per technique fires on 23.1%.

On a seeded test tenant built from fixtures shaped like Microsoft Graph data (not a live tenant), 14 read only checks found all 15 planted findings from 14 misconfigurations with 0 false findings, each mapped to the OWASP NHI Top 10.
On hosts updated but not restarted, 138 of 138 scanner verdicts (100.0%) said fixed while the old vulnerable code was still running; 2 of 2 scanners did so every time.

1,561,800 numbered canaries written through rsyslog and journald on an Ubuntu 24.04 host and counted again in Elasticsearch across 25 conditions: default pipelines lost up to 84.8% (Fluent Bit, Elasticsearch stopped for 10 min), and 82 of 124 lossy streams left no log line anywhere saying events were lost.
